HEEWON STYLE — a KOREAN WEBTOON movie still PAINTED like a premium digital painting, the look of a dramatic manhwa cover. A 2:1 movie frame composed for a 2:1 letterbox crop (nothing important at the top or bottom edge). The shot the scene names (wide establishing, two-shot, close-up, over-the-shoulder) from a dramatic camera angle (low three-quarter, worm's-eye, high overhead or dutch), never a flat straight-on catalogue pose. Named characters' FACES are drawn exactly like the attached character sheet: the same confident ink linework drawn BOLD and THICK with real line weight — a heavy tapered black contour around the whole silhouette and the hair mass, medium lines for folds and features, fine lines only for lashes and loose strands and manhwa face design (eye shape, brows, nose, jaw, hairline and hair), recognisably those characters, in the clothes the scene gives them. EVERYTHING ELSE IS PAINTED: visible textured brushwork — loose digital-paint strokes and dry-brush, charcoal-like hatching that follow every fold of the silk and every plate of armour, the shadows built from layered strokes, the brightest ridges laid in with single confident strokes, a faint paper-and-canvas grain; at the edges of the garments the linework breaks into loose sketchy strokes. NOT flat cel-shading, NOT smooth airbrushed gradients, NOT a clean vector look, NOT photoreal, NOT 3D. Dawn, wide, the camera low on the bow of a Tang tower-ship: its dark carved prow and a soldier’s back in steel lamellar sharp in the foreground, spray bursting over the bow. Ahead and on every side, the fleet: dozens of red-sailed tower-ships and warships at true size, hulls lined with tiny soldiers, oars beating, receding into gold haze. On the horizon the dark cliff-ridge of Bisa with its fortress wall along the crest. Wind, spray and banners in motion; awe on the soldier’s half-turned face. PLACE (match the battle map): the end of the Liaodong cape in early summer — a steep dark ridge with grey cliffs on every side and a Goguryeo stone fortress wall along its crest, a narrow inlet under it, a wide grey bay opening south to the sea. The Tang fleet of five hundred hulls comes up from the south out of the sea haze; a handful of Goguryeo warships row out of the inlet to meet it. Alongside, the Tang deck stands two men higher than the Goguryeo deck. BANNERS BY SIDE: vermilion Tang banners fly ONLY on the dark Tang hulls; red three-legged-crow banners ONLY on the Goguryeo ships; Tang sails are plain deep red, no emblem; the Tang sun disc holds an abstract black smudge, never a readable character. Goguryeo men in steel lamellar with red shoulder-wings and pheasant-feather helm plumes; Tang men in steel lamellar with vermilion cloth and round chest discs. REFERENCE SHEET. TOP ROW, left to right: ship_tang (copy its exact shape), ship_goguryeo (copy its exact shape), banner goguryeo (field colour and emblem for that side's war-banners). Kingdom banners: copy field colour and emblem from the attached flag_*.png ref onto period silk war-banners — tall poles behind each side, long streamers, small pennants on spear-tips and saddle-backs. Painted silk, wind-whipped, torn and smoke-stained in battle; never a flat modern flag graphic. Each side's banner colour is the clearest colour on its half of the frame, so the kingdom reads at a glance. Tang banners: vermilion silk with a yellow sun disc and a dark brush glyph inside it — painted as an illegible brush mark, never readable text. Attached flag /flag_tang.png. Goguryeo banners: red silk with the black three-legged crow inside a studded black sun-ring. Attached flag /flag_goguryeo.png. SHIPS: copy the attached ship board for each kingdom exactly (hull shape, mast count, sail colour and battens) and keep that same ship in every still of the scene. Boards are design only: ignore their bright daylight sky and calm sea, repaint the ship in the scene light. 7th-century timber ships only, never European hulls, cannon or funnels. TRUE SCALE (real 7th-century measures; a man is 1.65 m): ships are drawn life-size against their crews and against each other, never toy boats with giant men. A man standing on deck is about 1/15 the length of a 24 m warship and 1/20 of a 35 m tower-ship; a deck bulwark reaches his chest; the waterline is two men's height below a warship deck. Dozens of men fit along one side of a warship, each one small against the hull, masts four or five men tall. When two kingdoms' ships share a frame, keep their real length ratio. Tang louchuan tower-ship: huge dark timber hull with a multi-storey deck castle, two or three masts of deep red battened sails, the largest ship on any sea. Size: the flagship tower-ship is about 35 m long and 8–9 m wide, deck about 3 m above the water, its three-storey castle rising about 12 m (seven men tall), up to two hundred men aboard; the ordinary Tang warship is about 24 m long with forty to ninety men, its deck a man's height higher than any Yamato or Baekje boat. Its broadside looks like a city wall. Goguryeo warship: long high-sided timber hull with an oar-port gallery along the side, raised stern castle, three masts with cream battened sails, red Goguryeo banners at the stern. Size: about 25 m long and 6 m wide, deck about 2.5 m above the water, stern castle two storeys, about sixty men aboard; a little shorter and lower than a Tang tower-ship, about the size of a Tang ordinary warship. BACKGROUND AND LIGHT (painterly tenebrism): the background IS the place and the moment of the scene — open sky if they are in the sky, the hall if they are in a hall, the gate, the river, the snow — painted loosely in atmospheric brushwork (drifting smoke, cloud, haze, mist, falling snow, embers) in the scene's own colours, soft and out of focus, with a faint bokeh of small lights; it has colour, weather and depth — never a flat black void, never a detailed set; crowds and armies only as massed painted shapes dissolving into haze. ONE hard directional key light that belongs to the place (a brazier, a lamp, the sun through cloud, a torch, moonlight) rakes across the faces and clothes from the side or from below, modelling them in high contrast with deep painted shadows and a thin edge of the same light along the silhouette. Each character's colour lives in that light and in the atmosphere around them — never a glow aura or halo. Faces and bodies act the beat: real expressions, real weight, mid-motion. Faces from the sheet; new poses, never the sheet's stance. Each named person appears once, never cloned. Everyone wears period clothing of their own court (Korean, Tang, Yamato, Mohe furs), never European dress. No text, no speech bubbles, no panel borders, no watermark. DAY GROUND: the frame is built on WHITE — a high-key, paper-white ground: pale bright sky, white haze and mist, sunlit plaster and pale stone dissolving into bare white paper at the edges, the shadows few, crisp and cool-grey; the figure is the dark, inked thing in a bright frame. Never a black void, never a dim dusk wash.
